case_study_insert.main_stem: Hartwell Modular Homes (HMH) is a public limited company in the construction sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 2011 by Owen Hartwell, the business designs, manufactures and installs timber-frame modular houses for housing associations and private developers, and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. HMH plans to invest $2,300,000 in acquiring the assets of Fenwick Timber Frame, an insolvent modular rival in administration, financed by a $1,600,000 share issue and a $700,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $1,620,000 a year, a variable cost of $96,000 a unit and a selling price of $150,000, and currently produces 60 units a year. HMH faces two problems: a skills shortage, with 22 of 120 staff needing erector certification, and absenteeism has reached 7%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Q3 2026: HMH completed 15 timber-frame house assemblies last quarter; the remedial-work (defect) rate fell to 2.7% from 4.2% a year ago. Average foundation-to-handover time fell from 9.5 to 7.5 weeks. Market research of 320 housing-association buyers found 58% prioritise modular speed and 46% want a net-zero specification. Erector certification costs $1,200 per person; 22 of 120 staff need it. HMH's order book covers 48 houses to be delivered by March 2027.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Hartwell Modular Homes for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 5.25% to 6.0%, its third rise this year, increasing mortgage and development-finance costs. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $12.60 to $13.34 per hour from April 2027, raising assembly payroll costs. (3) Structural timber and panel import costs have risen 10.8% year-on-year, while planning approvals for new homes grew 4.6% in the same period.

questions.question_text: HMH plans to finance part of the Fenwick Timber Frame acquisition with a $1,600,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for HMH of using a share issue rather than relying solely on a bank loan for the $2,300,000 acquisition.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue raises permanent capital with no fixed interest or repayment schedule, so HMH is not committed to servicing a $2,300,000 bank loan on top of its existing $1,620,000 fixed costs and $410,000 interest payable. That keeps cash flow flexible while the insolvent Fenwick Timber Frame is integrated, protects the 48-house order book to March 2027, and guarantees the capital stays in the business indefinitely rather than being repaid at an inconvenient time.

Point 2: A larger share issue reduces default risk and spreads the acquisition's risk across new investors instead of loading it onto HMH's existing lenders. Unlike a bigger loan, it cannot trigger default, covenant breaches or a forced sale of Fenwick's assets if house completions slip, and it preserves borrowing capacity for a later overdraft or development finance needed to deliver the net-zero specification that 46% of surveyed housing-association buyers want — at a moment when planning approvals are growing only 4.6% and caution is prudent.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Hartwell Modular Homes and its acquisition decision.

questions.question_text: HMH is launching its net-zero timber-frame modular range to housing associations. Consider a national television campaign, sponsorship of a regional housing expo, or a targeted social-media campaign using home-tour case-study videos. Which should HMH choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television campaign: Television would reach millions quickly and make HMH a household name, which could impress prospective buyers and council planners. However, a plc of 120 employees cannot easily justify production and national airtime of hundreds of thousands of dollars, most viewers are not housing-association decision-makers, and the message cannot be targeted to the 58% of buyers prioritising modular speed or the 46% wanting net-zero specification.

Sponsorship of a regional housing expo: A branded stand at the Expo would put HMH face to face with housing-association procurement officers, let them walk through a finished module, and generate qualified leads in two days. Drawbacks: high stand and staffing cost, one-off reach, and rival exhibitors competing for the same 320-survey audience, so awareness decays fast after the event.

Targeted social-media campaign: Short home-tour videos on LinkedIn and Instagram aimed at housing associations and developers can show 7.5-week handover times, the 2.7% defect rate and net-zero features, cost far less than television, and be measured click by click. Risks: slower to build reach, dependent on content quality, and may under-reach older procurement officers who do not use social media heavily.

Recommendation: HMH should choose the targeted social-media campaign. It matches the B2B audience identified in HMH's research, costs a fraction of television, scales nationally unlike a one-off expo, and directly showcases the speed and net-zero differentiators. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for HMH's budget; the expo is rejected as a useful supporting event but cannot sustain awareness or reach beyond its two days, so social media should lead with the expo as a complement.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of HMH with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of HMH with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and the expo sponsorship are rejected as sole channels.

questions.question_text: HMH's absenteeism has reached 7% and 22 of 120 staff need erector certification. Explain two benefits for HMH of its flat organisational structure with democratic leadership.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A flat structure shortens the chain of command, so shop-floor feedback about defect hotspots (2.7%) and certification blockers reaches Owen Hartwell and site managers directly, cutting the delay between spotting a problem on the assembly line and fixing it. Fewer management layers also reduce overhead within the $1,620,000 fixed costs, which protects margins while the $2,300,000 Fenwick integration absorbs management attention and keeps decisions close to the 60 units produced a year.

Point 2: Democratic leadership gives assembly and erection crews a genuine voice in shift patterns, certification scheduling and problem-solving, satisfying their esteem and social needs (Maslow) and raising commitment. Workers who help plan the erector-certification rollout for the 22 uncertified staff are more likely to attend — directly attacking the 7% absenteeism — and more willing to share practical fixes that keep the 48-house order book on schedule for March 2027 delivery, propose net-zero ideas unprompted, and accept flexible cover when colleagues are absent.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HMH's absenteeism, certification gap and delivery pipeline.

questions.question_text: HMH wants to improve motivation and retention in its assembly teams. Consider performance-related bonuses or job enrichment. Which should HMH choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Performance-related bonuses: A bonus tied to on-time module completion and defect rates would give HMH's assembly crews a direct financial incentive to hit targets, suiting Taylor-style motivation and aligning pay with the 48-house order book. It is measurable, flexible and cheap when performance is good. However, it risks shortcuts on quality and safety, conflicts with the democratic culture Owen Hartwell has built with a workforce raised on involvement, and cannot substitute for the $1,200 erector certification that 22 of 120 staff still need before they can lawfully erect modules.

Job enrichment: Widening roles so assemblers own complete modules — from timber cutting to final inspection — adds responsibility, skill variety and recognition, feeding Herzberg's motivators and Maslow's esteem needs. This fits HMH's net-zero ambition (46% of buyers want it), builds multi-skilled erectors internally, deepens pride in defects falling to 2.7%, and reduces labour turnover without constant pay rises against fixed costs of $1,620,000 a year. Drawbacks: slower to feel than a cash bonus, needs training investment upfront, and some workers may resist wider duties or expect higher base pay.

Decision: HMH should choose job enrichment, supported by a modest team-based bonus for hitting handover deadlines. Money alone would not fix satisfaction or skills gaps; enrichment addresses the root causes of absenteeism (7%) and disengagement while building the certified erector capability the order book needs. Performance bonuses alone are rejected because they reward speed over quality, may push the defect rate back up, erode the democratic culture, and cannot replace the certification training that is the binding constraint on delivery.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two motivation methods with limited application to HMH.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both motivation methods in the context of HMH.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both motivation methods in the context of HMH with a well-justified decision covering cost, quality, retention and skills development.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how HMH's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $1,620,000 ÷ ($150,000 − $96,000) = $1,620,000 ÷ $54,000 = 30 units. Answer: break-even output is 30 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $150,000 − $96,000 = $54,000. Answer: contribution per unit is $54,000.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways HMH's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. HMH's managers can compare the 30-unit break-even output with actual output of 60 units to confirm the Fenwick acquisition is above the profit threshold, with a margin of safety of 30 houses, informing whether to raise production capacity further.
2. Contribution per unit of $54,000 lets HMH model developer discounts: for example, cutting the price to $142,000 drops contribution to $46,000, so managers can judge whether the volume gain covers the $1,620,000 fixed costs before repricing the order book.
3. The unit cost of $123,000 a unit ($7,380,000 total costs ÷ 60 units) lets managers benchmark performance quarter by quarter, expose waste in timber usage against the 10.8% import-cost inflation, and set lamination standards for the acquired Fenwick plant.
4. Knowing break-even output helps managers set completion targets for the 48-house order book, check the $700,000 bank loan can be serviced comfortably, and decide whether the remaining $1,600,000 share issue is sufficient for the integration programme.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $54,000 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: 30-house margin of safety against 60-unit output; discount modelling at $54,000 contribution; unit cost benchmarking at $123,000 against timber inflation; and loan-servicing checks on the $700,000 bank loan and $2,300,000 acquisition.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HMH's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has HMH's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 30.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 32.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 16.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 20.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit = $7,800,000 revenue − $5,460,000 cost of sales = $2,340,000; 2025 gross profit = $9,000,000 revenue − $6,120,000 cost of sales = $2,880,000. Operating profit rose from $1,170,000 to $1,440,000. Capital employed rose from $6,500,000 to $7,200,000. 2024: $2,340,000 ÷ $7,800,000 = 30.0%; $1,170,000 ÷ $7,800,000 = 15.0%; $1,170,000 ÷ $6,500,000 = 18.0%. 2025: $2,880,000 ÷ $9,000,000 = 32.0%; $1,440,000 ÷ $9,000,000 = 16.0%; $1,440,000 ÷ $7,200,000 = 20.0%.

Evaluation: Performance has improved, though only modestly. Revenue grew by $1,200,000 to $9,000,000 (+$1,200,000 ÷ $7,800,000 × 100 = 15.4%) and gross profit rose by $540,000 (+$540,000 ÷ $2,340,000 × 100 = 23.1%), and return on capital employed rose despite capital employed also growing — the acquisition is beginning to pay. However, interest payable climbed from $340,000 to $410,000 (+$70,000; $70,000 ÷ $340,000 × 100 = 20.6%), suggesting debt service is eating into gains; the timber import-cost rise of 10.8% threatens 2026 cost of sales; and the defect rate, though down to 2.7%, still drives remedial expense. The improvements of 2 percentage points on each measure are real but thin for a company that has just taken on a $700,000 loan for Fenwick.

Conclusion: HMH's financial performance has improved. Revenue, gross profit, operating profit and every ratio (30.0% to 32.0%, 15.0% to 16.0%, 18.0% to 20.0%) moved upward. The improvement is not yet spectacular relative to the scale of the acquisition, so HMH must deliver the 48-house order book on time and control timber and interest costs to lock in the gains.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, operating profit and capital employed movements and a justified conclusion on whether HMH's financial performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HMH of acquiring Fenwick Timber Frame out of administration.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Acquiring the assets of Fenwick Timber Frame, an insolvent modular rival in administration, for $2,300,000 allows HMH to put the capacity of a failed rival to work quickly instead of building from scratch, removing a competitor from the timber-frame market and protecting HMH's ability to deliver its 48-house order book to housing associations — 46% of 320 surveyed buyers want a net-zero specification that suits HMH's product. General takeover-finance reasoning favours the deal too: HMH can fold the assets into its existing organisation and finance most of the $2,300,000 with permanent equity rather than further bank debt, preserving the $700,000 loan and the $1,600,000 share issue for operations.

Disadvantage: The acquisition commits HMH to a $2,300,000 outlay financed by a $1,600,000 share issue and a $700,000 bank loan, diluting existing shareholders and adding interest on top of the $410,000 already payable. Because Fenwick failed in administration, the assets HMH is buying may carry hidden liabilities — unfinished work, disputed contracts, deferred maintenance — that only surface after handover, while HMH's management team of 120 people must integrate Fenwick without letting the 7% absenteeism, the 2.7% defect rate or the 9.5-to-7.5-week handover timetable slip.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HMH's acquisition, costs and operational position.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 6.0%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 10.8% rise in timber import costs will affect HMH. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.25% to 6.0%): On the $700,000 bank loan, 0.75 points adds roughly $5,250 a year, and interest payable (already $410,000 and rising) will climb further. More damaging is the demand side: at 6.0%, housing-association development finance and buyer mortgages cost more, so planning approvals (up 4.6%) may slow into 2027, threatening HMH's 48-house order book and the net-zero pipeline. HMH can fix the loan at renewal, but cannot fix the market.

Minimum wage rise (5.9%, to $13.34 per hour from April 2027): The award adds exactly $0.74 per hour for every minimum-wage hour ($13.34 − $12.60). The insert does not state per-worker hours, so the annual total cannot be fixed precisely, but the effect scales across 120 staff; illustratively, if all 120 averaged 1,000 minimum-wage hours each a year, the award would add 120 × 1,000 × $0.74 = $88,800 a year — a material payroll increase beside fixed costs of $1,620,000 a year, made heavier by the 7% absenteeism that already forces cover, and by the $1,200 certification bill for 22 uncertified staff. HMH can partly offset it with productivity gains from the Fenwick acquisition.

Timber import-cost inflation (10.8% year-on-year): The insert states structural timber and panel import costs rose 10.8% year-on-year but does not split the $96,000 variable cost into timber and non-timber components, so the exact annual effect cannot be isolated. What can be quantified: every $10,000 of timber content within the $96,000 variable cost rises by $1,080 per unit ($10,000 × 10.8%); across 60 units that is $64,800 a year per $10,000 of timber content. Illustratively, if half the variable cost were timber — $48,000 per unit, a deliberately generous bound rather than an insert figure — the rise would add $5,184 per unit ($48,000 × 10.8%), or $311,040 a year ($5,184 × 60). Even a quarter share ($24,000) would add $2,592 per unit ($24,000 × 10.8%), or $155,520 a year. Either bound dwarfs the rate rise, and the pressure compounds across HMH's 48-house backlog and cannot be passed on quickly in fixed-price contracts with housing associations.

Conclusion: The 10.8% timber import-cost inflation will have the greatest impact. It strikes directly at HMH's core input, compounds across the 48-house backlog, cannot be passed on quickly in fixed-price contracts with housing associations, and at even a quarter-share illustrative bound reaches roughly $155,520 a year — far above the labelled $88,800 wage-bound illustration and the roughly $5,250 a year rate effect ($700,000 × 0.75%). The wage increase is second (a $0.74 per hour award on every minimum-wage hour, offsetable through productivity); the rate rise is smallest in direct cash but carries the biggest demand risk for approvals growing 4.6%. HMH must renegotiate material supply contracts, dual-source timber regionally and re-price new tenders urgently.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to HMH.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on HMH's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of HMH with a well-justified judgement that timber import-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
